<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
			<title>The beginning of the 7.3 merge window</title>
			<link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1089244/</link>
			<guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1089244/</guid>
			<dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
			<description>As of this writing, 2,346 non-merge changesets have been pulled into the
mainline repository for the 7.3 kernel release.  That, clearly, is a mere
down payment on the flood that is to come.  Even so, those early pulls
brought in some noteworthy changes, including (but not limited to) a
significant reworking of how group scheduling works on multiprocessor
systems.
</description>
			<pubDate>Thu, 03 Sep 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
		</item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
			<title>A look at the Quickshell desktop-component toolkit</title>
			<link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1083090/</link>
			<guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1083090/</guid>
			<dc:creator>jzb</dc:creator>
			<description><p><a href="https://quickshell.org/">Quickshell</a> is a toolkit for
building desktop components, such as toolbars or menus. It uses <a
href="https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qmlreference.html">QML</a>, which is a declarative language
for designing GUI applications. Quickshell helps developers create graphical tools
for common desktop use cases with a focus on ease of development. It offers a
convenient method for writing user interfaces and has been adopted by a number
of projects, such as <a
href="https://github.com/caelestia-dots/shell#caelestia-shell">caelestia-shell</a> and <a href="https://danklinux.com/">DankMaterialShell</a>, that
provide desktop environments for minimal window managers like <a
href="https://swaywm.org/">Sway</a> and <a
href="https://niri-wm.github.io/niri/">niri</a>.</p>
</description>
			<pubDate>Thu, 03 Sep 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
		</item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
			<title>Considering the OpenMDW license</title>
			<link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1089251/</link>
			<guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1089251/</guid>
			<dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
			<description>The open-source world has been struggling for a few years now to understand
how to approach large language models (LLMs) and the licensing applied to
them.  What constitutes "freedom" with respect to a black box filled with
numerical weights?  The process taken by the Open Source Initiative (OSI)
in the <a href="https://lwn.net/Articles/995159/">development</a> of its <a
href="https://opensource.org/ai/open-source-ai-definition">Open Source AI
Definition</a> was controversial at best, as was its output.  Now, the
Linux Foundation's Mike Dolan has <a
href="https://lwn.net/ml/all/CAFV=PSG=bsLTemzjyCKYYz9j=rX9dcNo6=2T6htbxTRgervMrA@mail.gmail.com">brought
a new license to the OSI</a> for approval.  It is called the OpenMDW ("Open
Model, Data, and Weights"), and it aims to clarify licensing for the
distribution of LLMs and related materials, but consensus is proving hard
to find for this license as well.
</description>
			<pubDate>Thu, 03 Sep 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
		</item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
			<title>How to be safe from quantum computing</title>
			<link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1088305/</link>
			<guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1088305/</guid>
			<dc:creator>daroc</dc:creator>
			<description><p>
Practical quantum computers have been ten years away for the last several
decades. Now, however, it's beginning to look as though they will be
possible in just a few years. Recent
<a href="https://lwn.net/Articles/1066156/">
research with obfuscated results</a> demonstrated much lower memory requirements to factor
<a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic_Curve_Digital_Signature_Algorithm">
ECDSA</a> keys on a quantum computer, with
<a href="https://www.ecdsa.fail/">
work by other researchers in the open</a> more than halving memory use compared
to the state of the art in 2023.
At the same time, computer
manufacturers are
<a href="https://abit.ee/en/processors/ibm-quantum-processor-nighthawk-ibm-miami-quantum-computing-qubits-coherence-heron-r3-quantum-advant-en">
boasting</a> quantum processors that retain viable superpositions over longer periods.
Given how slowly software updates filter out to stable systems, it's worth
looking at what configuration changes and protocol updates are needed to be safe
from quantum computers now.
</p>
</description>
			<pubDate>Thu, 03 Sep 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
		</item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
			<title>Old-school calendaring at the command line with Remind</title>
			<link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1090376/</link>
			<guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1090376/</guid>
			<dc:creator>jzb</dc:creator>
			<description><p><a href="https://dianne.skoll.ca/projects/remind/">Remind</a> is a
command-line calendar and alarm program, with an optional Tk-based graphical
interface, for Linux and Unix-like operating systems. It has its own scripting
language that allows users to create reminders that are difficult (if not
impossible) to specify in other calendaring programs. It is wholly unsuitable for use in
corporate environments that require calendar sharing and exchanging meeting
invitations; however, it may be precisely the calendaring tool for users who
prefer the command line and fast, flexible tools that can help keep track of
messy schedules.</p>
</description>
			<pubDate>Thu, 03 Sep 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
		</item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
			<title>An ongoing 3D-printer AGPL violation</title>
			<link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1089390/</link>
			<guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1089390/</guid>
			<dc:creator>jake</dc:creator>
			<description>At <a href="https://2026.fossy.ca/">FOSSY 2026</a>, several people from the
<a href="https://sfconservancy.org/">Software Freedom Conservancy</a> (SFC),
which organizes the conference, gave a presentation about an <a href="https://sfconservancy.org/news/2026/may/18/bambu-studio-3d-printer-agpl-violation-response/">ongoing
violation</a> of the <a
href="https://www.gnu.org/licenses/agpl-3.0.en.html">Affero General Public
License version 3</a> (AGPLv3).  Bradley Kühn, Karen Sandler, and Denver
Gingerich spoke about different aspects of the violation, which is in
regard to 3D-printer software from Bambu Lab, and what is being
done to try to provide users with alternatives.  One aspect that is
particularly interesting is that the circumvention that the company is
employing is precisely what the AGPL was written to prevent.
</description>
			<pubDate>Thu, 03 Sep 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
		</item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>Using steal time to moderate CPU demands</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1090381/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1090381/</guid>
        <dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
        <description>Virtualization can increase CPU utilization by allowing a large number of
virtual CPUs to share a smaller number of physical CPUs.  The amount of CPU
time that is actually available does not change, though, so heavy activity
on too many virtual CPUs can lead to contention and significant performance
loss.  The <a
href="https://lwn.net/ml/all/20260825103855.721013-1-sshegde@linux.ibm.com">steal governor
patch series</a> from Shrikanth Hegde is an attempt to address that problem
with a mechanism that allows virtual machines to voluntarily reduce the
number of virtual CPUs they use when contention is high.
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 10 Sep 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>The "rnull" Rust block driver</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1090378/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1090378/</guid>
        <dc:creator>daroc</dc:creator>
        <description><p>
The
<a href="https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/block/null_blk.html">null block
driver</a> (<tt>null_blk</tt>)
is a small driver that is mostly useful for benchmarking block-layer
implementations. It accepts all requests and marks them complete as quickly as
possible, doing as little work as possible. In June&#160;2026, Andreas Hindborg shared
<a href="https://lwn.net/ml/all/20260609-rnull-v6-19-rc5-send-v2-0-82c7404542e2@kernel.org/">
a patch set</a> implementing the same functionality in Rust, in order to show
that a simple block driver is now possible to write using the kernel's
Rust APIs and to enable comparisons between the C and Rust
implementations.
A minimal version of the "rnull" driver is already present in the mainline
kernel, but Hindborg's patch set brings it up to feature parity with the C
version.
</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 10 Sep 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>The rest of the 7.3 merge window</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1089791/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1089791/</guid>
        <dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
        <description>By the time Linus Torvalds <a
href="https://lwn.net/ml/all/CAHk-=wjpN3XkKU+JX6zoh_bzJXr1aPYN4FY14UX0z7yCidosPQ@mail.gmail.com/">released
7.3-rc1</a> and closed the merge window for this release, 15,267 non-merge
changesets had been pulled into the mainline repository.  That is the
second-highest commit count for an -rc1 release in the kernel's history;
only the 6.7-rc1 release, which included nearly 3,000 commits of bcachefs
history, had more.  About 13,000 of those commits entered the mainline
after <a href="https://lwn.net/Articles/1089244/">the first 7.3 merge-window summary</a>
was written so, needless to say, there are a lot of changes to cover.
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 10 Sep 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>A pause for the Python JIT</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1090385/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1090385/</guid>
        <dc:creator>jzb</dc:creator>
        <description><p>In 2024 the <a
href="https://www.python.org/downloads/release/python-3130/">Python&#160;3.13</a>
release added an <a
href="https://docs.python.org/3.13/whatsnew/3.13.html#an-experimental-just-in-time-jit-compiler">experimental
just-in-time (JIT) compiler</a> to optimize the way that CPython executes Python
code. Since then, work has proceeded on the JIT, albeit perhaps less formally
than some might like. In June, Python's <a
href="https://peps.python.org/pep-0013/#the-steering-council">steering
council</a> (SC) put out an <a
href="https://discuss.python.org/t/an-announcement-from-the-steering-council-regarding-the-jit-project/107638">announcement</a>
that no new development on the JIT land (with the exception of bug and security
fixes) in Python's main branch, until it accepts a <a
href="https://peps.python.org/pep-0001">Python Enhancement Proposal</a> (PEP)
that would make the case for the JIT as a supported part of CPython. That has
led to the creation of <a
href="https://peps.python.org/pep-0836/">PEP&#160;836</a> ("JIT Go Brrr: The
Path to a Supported JIT Compiler for CPython"), which is currently under
discussion. As it stands, it seems likely that work on JIT will continue, but
when that will happen is less certain.</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 10 Sep 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>Governing GNOMEs: how the project's technical decision-making is evolving</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1091619/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1091619/</guid>
        <dc:creator>jzb</dc:creator>
        <description><p>Emmanuele Bassi kicked off a project to improve GNOME's technical governance
with a <a href="https://lwn.net/Articles/1034684/">presentation about his
ideas</a> (<a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=n3SviPlMyhM">video</a>) at
<a href="https://events.gnome.org/event/259/">GUADEC&#160;2025</a>. His nudging
has led the project to, slowly, work on creating more formal structures for
technical governance. It is adopting a teams structure and looking toward
creating a steering committee, as well as bootstrapping a Request for Comments
(RFC) process. If adopted, GNOME would require RFCs for design, user experience,
architectural, and other changes that carry a major impact on the project.</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 10 Sep 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>Securely suspending LUKS-encrypted disks</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1090568/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1090568/</guid>
        <dc:creator>daroc</dc:creator>
        <description><p>
When a laptop is asleep, its memory is not unreadable. The right
tooling can attach to the computer's memory bus and read out its contents, and
<a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_boot_attack">
cold-boot attacks</a> can theoretically read values from memory for a short time
after the computer loses power. That
is really an unavoidable fact about the hardware, but some users would still
like to ensure that, even if this happens, their long-term encryption keys, such as
the key for full-disk encryption, remain unreadable. In June&#160;2026, Ingo
Blechschmidt
<a href="https://mathstodon.xyz/@iblech/116769502749142438">
discovered</a> that Linux kernel versions after 6.9 (released in
May&#160;2024)
were not erasing disk-encryption keys when a laptop was put to sleep, even
when configured to do so. He quickly identified a potential fix, which has been
merged, but it was not a comprehensive solution.
</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 10 Sep 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>Recent work in memory tiering</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1092001/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1092001/</guid>
        <dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
        <description>Tiered-memory systems are built with multiple types of memory, each of
which has different performance characteristics.  In addition to the usual
DRAM, a tiered system might also provide faster high-bandwidth memory or
slower CXL memory.  On these systems, the placement of memory allocations
has a significant effect on the performance that a workload will obtain.
While work on tiered-memory improvements has been ongoing for years, it
feels like the pace has slowed a bit recently.  Even so, there are a few
efforts underway, but they are facing questions about whether the tiering
design makes sense.
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 17 Sep 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>Deterministic testing for multithreaded Python</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1090579/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1090579/</guid>
        <dc:creator>jake</dc:creator>
        <description>Python's support for multithreaded programs has improved considerably over
the last few years with the advent of the <a
href="https://lwn.net/Articles/1078367/">"free-threaded" version of the language</a>.  But
testing multithreaded programs is notoriously difficult, because the
underlying host system determines the thread-execution ordering, which adds
an element of non-determinism.  At PyCon US, Larry Hastings gave a talk (<a
href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=S3LUpx0hzkw&t=96s">YouTube video</a>)
about his <a href="https://pypi.org/project/blanket/">blanket</a> project,
which is meant to provide mechanisms for deterministic testing of
multithreaded Python code.
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 17 Sep 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>
